PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

The descant recorder is a small wind instrument played with the mouth and the fingers. In this sub-strand you will name its parts, learn how to keep it clean and store it safely, and play the notes B, A and G with a good posture and a gentle breath. You will then play simple tunes on those three notes and listen to one another.

## Strand 2.0: Performing and Displaying
Sub-strand 2.5: Descant Recorder
Suggested lessons: 15

## What this sub-strand covers
• Parts: head joint, middle joint, foot joint, finger holes
• Care: hygiene measures, handling and storage
• Techniques: posture, fingering and blowing

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 Creative Arts Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Strand 2.0 Performing and Displaying, Sub-strand 2.5 Descant Recorder

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) identify the parts of a descant recorder for familiarisation
b) care for a descant recorder for longevity
c) play notes B A and G on a descant recorder using appropriate playing techniques
d) play simple melodies based on notes B A and G on the descant recorder
e) enjoy playing melodies using the descant recorder

## Key inquiry questions
1. How can a good tone be produced on the descant recorder?

PAGE 2: How we will learn

## Learning experiences
• familiarise with the descant recorder to identify its parts
• brainstorm on ways of caring for a descant recorder and its importance
• practise the techniques of playing a descant recorder
• use digital devices responsibly to search and watch recordings/ watch live demonstrations on how to play notes B A and G on the descant recorder
• play simple melodies based on B A and G on the descant recorder with accuracy in pitch and rhythm applying the playing techniques
• watch peers play melodies on the descant recorder, critique and give feedback to peers for improvement

## Core competencies
• Digital literacy: The learner uses digital devices to search and watch how to play notes on the descant recorder
• Learning to learn: The learner searches for and acquires skills of how to play new notes on the descant recorder

## Values
• Respect: The learner listens to and accommodates peers’ views during discussions
• Responsibility: The learner takes care of the descant recorder during and after use

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Communicable diseases: The learner prevents the spread of communicable diseases by observing hygiene measures in the use of the descant recorder
• Social cohesion: The learner plays the descant recorder with peers in a group

## Links to other learning areas
• Agriculture: The learner applies the concepts and knowledge learnt on prevention of communicable diseases in the use of the descant recorder

PAGE 3: Lesson 1: Parts of the descant recorder — The three joints

LESSON 1: PARTS OF THE DESCANT RECORDER
=======================================

## What you will learn
• Name the head joint, middle joint, foot joint and finger holes.
• Assemble the recorder so the holes line up.
• Hold it the right way up before any playing.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify the parts of a descant recorder for familiarisation

## Introduction
A descant recorder looks like one tube, but it comes apart into pieces. If you do not know which piece is which, you cannot put it together or find the notes.

## Notes

The descant recorder is the small recorder most schools use. It is sometimes called a soprano recorder. Sound is made by blowing gently into the mouthpiece while fingers cover and uncover holes. Covering more holes makes a lower note.

### The three joints
- The **head joint** is the top piece. It has the **beak** (the mouthpiece you rest on your lips) and the **window**, a rectangular opening underneath where the air splits and the sound begins.
- The **middle joint** is the long middle piece. Most of the finger holes are on it.
- The **foot joint** is the small bottom piece. It has the last hole, often a double hole.

### Finger holes
The holes on the front are covered by the fingers. The hole at the back of the head joint, or at the top of the middle joint depending on the model, is covered by the left thumb. You do not need every hole yet. Notes B, A and G use only the left thumb and the first fingers of the left hand. The other holes still have to be there, and you must not block them by mistake.

PAGE 4: Lesson 1: Parts of the descant recorder — Example 2

### Putting it together
Fit the foot joint onto the middle joint, then fit the head joint. Use a gentle twist. Do not force the pieces or bang them on a desk. The window of the head joint should line up with the finger holes. If the head joint faces sideways, your fingers will not sit on the holes.

Left hand goes at the top, nearer the beak. Right hand goes at the bottom. If you swap hands, the notes B, A and G will not work. Look at a chart or a real recorder and touch each part as you name it. Familiarity means you can name the parts without looking at a label.

## Key words
• descant recorder — a small recorder played by blowing and covering finger holes
• head joint — the top piece with the beak and the window
• middle joint — the long piece with most of the finger holes
• foot joint — the small bottom piece
• finger hole — an opening covered by a finger to change the note

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Which joint has the beak and the window?

Working:
1. The mouthpiece is at the top.
2. The top piece is the head joint.

Answer: The head joint.

## Worked examples

### Example 2
A learner puts the right hand at the top. What will go wrong?

Working:
1. The left hand must be nearer the beak.
2. Notes B, A and G use the left-hand fingers.

Answer: The fingers will be on the wrong holes, so B, A and G will not sound correctly.

PAGE 5: Lesson 2: Caring for the recorder — Hygiene

## Activity: Name and assemble
You will need: A descant recorder for each player or for each pair, A diagram or Baroque fingering chart

1. Take the recorder apart carefully.

2. Point to the head joint, middle joint, foot joint, beak, window and finger holes.

3. Assemble it with a gentle twist so the window lines up with the holes.

4. Place the left hand at the top and the right hand below, without playing yet.

5. Your partner checks the lineup and the hands.

## Practice

1. Name the three joints of a descant recorder from top to bottom.

2. What is the window?

3. Which hand goes nearer the beak?

## Answers to practice

1. Head joint, middle joint, foot joint.

2. The rectangular opening where the air splits and the sound begins.

3. The left hand.

## Summary
• The recorder has a head joint, a middle joint and a foot joint.
• Finger holes change the notes.
• Assemble it gently, with the left hand at the top.

LESSON 2: CARING FOR THE RECORDER
=================================

## What you will learn
• Clean and store a descant recorder correctly.
• Explain how hygiene stops germs spreading.
• Give two reasons why care makes the instrument last.

Curriculum outcomes: b) care for a descant recorder for longevity

## Introduction
A recorder goes in the mouth, so it is not like a drum that the whole class can hit in turn. How you clean it, hold it and put it away decides both its life and the health of the class.

## Notes

Care has two aims. Hygiene keeps germs from spreading. Gentle handling and storage make the recorder last. Lasting a long time is what longevity means.

### Hygiene
- Play only your own recorder. Do not lend the beak to a friend “just to try”.
- Wash your hands before you play.
- Do not play if you have a mouth infection, and do not share mouthpieces when someone has a cold or a cough. This helps prevent communicable diseases, the illnesses that pass from person to person.
- After playing, shake moisture out of the head joint. Wipe the beak.
- A plastic school recorder may be washed in lukewarm soapy water, rinsed and dried. Do not use boiling water. Do not leave it to soak all day.
- If your recorder is wooden, do not soak it. Wipe it and let it dry. Ask the teacher before washing any recorder that is not plastic.

PAGE 6: Lesson 2: Caring for the recorder — Example 1

### Handling
- Do not bite the beak.
- Do not bang the joints together or use the recorder as a pointer.
- Twist gently when you take it apart. Forcing a stuck joint can crack it.
- Carry it in your hand or case, not in a pocket full of pens.

### Storage
- Dry it before you put it away.
- Keep it in a case or a clean bag.
- Do not leave it in hot sun or on a window sill. Heat can warp plastic and crack wood.
- Store it where it will not be sat on.

A dirty, shared, sun-baked recorder becomes unpleasant to play and may not sound. A clean, personal, cool, dry recorder is ready for the next lesson.

## Key words
• hygiene — clean habits that stop germs spreading
• longevity — a long life; here, the recorder lasting a long time
• communicable disease — an illness that can pass from one person to another

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Two learners have a cold and want to try each other’s recorders. Why is that a poor idea?

Working:
1. Colds spread through shared mouthpieces.
2. Each player should use only their own recorder.

Answer: They could pass germs to each other. Each person should play only their own recorder.

## Worked examples

### Example 2
A plastic recorder was left on a hot window sill. What risk is that?

Working:
1. Heat can bend plastic.

Answer: The recorder may warp, so the joints and holes no longer fit well.

## Activity: Clean, dry and store
You will need: Own descant recorder, Lukewarm soapy water if the teacher says the recorder is plastic, Clean cloth, Case or clean bag

1. In a group, list ways of caring for the recorder and why each one matters.

2. Wash hands. If the recorder is plastic and the teacher agrees, wash it in lukewarm soapy water and rinse it.

3. Dry the joints and the beak.

4. Assemble it gently, then take it apart again and put it in the case.

5. Agree one class rule: nobody shares a mouthpiece.

PAGE 7: Lesson 3: Posture and how to hold the recorder — Body

## Practice

1. Why should learners not share recorder mouthpieces?

2. What water is safe for a plastic recorder?

3. Give two storage rules.

## Answers to practice

1. Germs that cause communicable diseases can spread from mouth to mouth.

2. Lukewarm soapy water, followed by a rinse and drying. Not boiling water.

3. Any two: dry it first, use a case or clean bag, keep it out of hot sun, do not leave it where it can be sat on.

## Summary
• Play only your own recorder and wash your hands.
• Wash a plastic recorder in lukewarm water, then dry it.
• Store it cool, dry and protected so it lasts.

LESSON 3: POSTURE AND HOW TO HOLD THE RECORDER
==============================================

## What you will learn
• Sit or stand with a playing posture.
• Place the left hand on top and seal the holes with the pads of the fingers.
• Support the recorder with the right hand without covering holes you do not need.

Curriculum outcomes: c) play notes B A and G on a descant recorder using appropriate playing techniques

## Introduction
A hunched back and flat fingers make the recorder squeak before the tune has started. Posture is the first playing technique.

## Notes

Posture means the way you sit or stand and the way you hold the instrument. A good posture lets the breath move and lets the fingers seal the holes.

### Body
- Sit toward the front of the chair, or stand with both feet on the ground.
- Keep the back tall, not stiff. The shoulders stay down.
- The head is level. Do not tuck the chin hard into the chest.
- Hold the recorder at a slant, pointing down and slightly forward, about halfway between straight up and straight out. It should not point at the floor between your feet, and it should not stick straight out like a stick.

### Hands
- Left hand on top. The left thumb covers the thumb hole at the back.
- The pads of the fingers, not the very tips and not the flat middle of the finger, cover the holes.
- Fingers are curved, as if each hand is holding a small ball.
- Right hand supports the lower joint. For notes B, A and G the right-hand fingers stay just above their holes, ready, but they do not cover them.
- Elbows hang relaxed. Do not glue them to your ribs and do not flap them out.

PAGE 8: Lesson 3: Posture and how to hold the recorder — Silent holding practice

### A seal test
Cover one hole and ask a partner to look around the finger. If they can see the hole, air will leak and the note will be wrong or noisy. Leaks are the main reason beginners think the recorder is broken.

Practise the holding shape in silence. Lifting and replacing one finger without looking at the hole is the skill you will need when the notes arrive. Keep the recorder out of your mouth until the next lesson, so that posture is learnt before blowing.

## Key words
• posture — the way you sit or stand and hold the instrument
• pad of the finger — the soft front of the fingertip that seals a hole
• seal — to cover a hole completely so air cannot leak

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner’s note will not sound and a partner can see half of hole 1. What is the cause?

Working:
1. A visible hole means air is leaking.
2. The pad of the finger must seal it.

Answer: The finger is not sealing the hole.

## Worked examples

### Example 2
Which hand is on top when playing B, A and G?

Working:
1. Those notes use the upper holes.
2. The left hand plays the upper holes.

Answer: The left hand.

## Activity: Silent holding practice
You will need: Descant recorder, Chair or standing space, A partner

1. Sit or stand tall and hold the recorder at a comfortable downward slant.

2. Place the left thumb and fingers in a curved shape. The right hand supports the bottom.

3. Your partner checks that the left hand is on top and that covered holes are fully sealed.

4. Lift one finger and replace it five times without twisting the recorder.

5. Rest the recorder in your lap or case. Nobody blows yet.

PAGE 9: Lesson 4: Blowing and a good tone

## Practice

1. Where should the left hand be?

2. Which part of the finger seals a hole?

3. What does the right hand do while you play B, A and G?

## Answers to practice

1. At the top, nearer the beak.

2. The pad of the finger.

3. It supports the lower part of the recorder and stays ready, without covering holes.

## Summary
• Sit or stand tall, with the recorder slanting gently downward.
• Left hand on top, fingers curved, holes sealed.
• The right hand supports the instrument for these three notes.

LESSON 4: BLOWING AND A GOOD TONE
=================================

## What you will learn
• Start a sound with the tongue.
• Use a gentle, steady breath.
• Explain what causes a squeak.

Curriculum outcomes: c) play notes B A and G on a descant recorder using appropriate playing techniques

## Introduction
The recorder does not need the huge breath you use to blow up a ball. It needs a small, steady stream of air, started neatly with the tongue.

## Notes

Tone is the quality of the sound: clear, gentle and steady, or squeaky, breathy and harsh. The question for this instrument is how a good tone is produced.

### The mouth
Rest the beak on the lower lip and close the lips gently around it. Do not bite. Only a small part of the beak goes into the mouth. The teeth do not clamp down. The cheeks stay flat, not puffed out.

PAGE 10: Lesson 4: Blowing and a good tone — A first sound

### The tongue
Start each note by saying “doo” or “too” inside the mouth. The tongue touches the back of the upper teeth and comes away as the air begins. This is called tonguing. It makes a clean start. Blowing without the tongue makes a fuzzy “whoosh”.

### The breath
Blow warm, slow air, as if you were steaming a mirror. If you blow hard, the recorder jumps to a high squeak. If you blow too little, you get a whisper and no note. Steady air in the middle is the tone you want.

### A first sound
Cover no front holes. Cover the thumb hole only if your teacher’s chart asks for that first open note. Many classes first practise a gentle tongued sound so the ears learn a clear tone before the fingers complicate it. If the sound squeaks:

- blow more gently
- check that you are not biting
- check for leaking fingers if any holes are covered
- check that the head joint window is lined up and not blocked by dirt

Stop every few minutes and let moisture out of the head joint. A blocked window gurgles. Good tone is gentle air, a tongued start, a sealed hole and a clear window.

PAGE 11: Lesson 4: Blowing and a good tone — Answers to practice

## Key words
• tone — the quality of the sound
• tonguing — starting a note with the tongue, as in “doo” or “too”
• squeak — a high unwanted sound caused by blowing too hard or by a leak

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Every note jumps to a high squeak. What should the player change first?

Working:
1. Hard blowing makes the recorder overblow.
2. The breath should be gentle and steady.

Answer: Blow more gently, with warm steady air.

## Worked examples

### Example 2
The sound starts with a fuzzy whoosh. Which technique is missing?

Working:
1. A clean start uses the tongue.
2. Saying “doo” or “too” is tonguing.

Answer: Tonguing.

## Activity: Gentle “doo” sounds
You will need: Own descant recorder

1. Check posture and a clean beak.

2. Practise saying “doo doo doo doo” on a gentle breath, four sounds, then rest.

3. If the sound squeaks, soften the breath and try again.

4. A partner says whether the tone was clear or forced.

5. Shake moisture out and rest the recorder.

## Practice

1. How can a good tone be produced on the descant recorder?

2. What happens if you blow too hard?

3. Should you bite the beak?

## Answers to practice

1. Use a gentle steady breath, start the note with the tongue, seal the holes, and keep the window clear.

2. The note squeaks or jumps too high.

3. No. The lips rest gently around it.

## Summary
• Lips rest gently on the beak. Do not bite or puff the cheeks.
• Start notes with “doo” or “too”.
• A gentle steady breath makes a clear tone.

PAGE 12: Lesson 5: Playing the note B — Steps

LESSON 5: PLAYING THE NOTE B
============================

## What you will learn
• Finger note B on a Baroque descant recorder.
• Play four steady B notes with a clear tone.
• Fix a leak or a squeak on B.

Curriculum outcomes: c) play notes B A and G on a descant recorder using appropriate playing techniques

## Introduction
B is the first of the three notes in this sub-strand. It uses the fewest fingers, so it is the best place to join posture, breath and a sealed hole.

## Notes

Use a Baroque fingering chart, the chart used with school descant recorders in this design. For note B, only two holes are covered:

- the left thumb covers the thumb hole at the back
- the left index finger covers hole 1, the first hole on the front

All the other holes stay open. The right hand still supports the recorder.

### Steps
1. Sit or stand tall. Left hand on top.
2. Seal the thumb hole and hole 1. Look once to check, then look forward.
3. Start with “doo” and a gentle breath.
4. Hold the note while you count “one”, then stop the air with the tongue.
5. Play four separate B notes: doo, doo, doo, doo. Keep them the same length.

PAGE 13: Lesson 5: Playing the note B — Four clean B notes

### If B will not sound
- The index finger is leaking. Seal with the pad.
- The thumb is only half on the hole.
- You are blowing too hard.
- You swapped hands.
- The head joint has twisted so the window is no longer in line.

Watch a live demonstration or a recording if the teacher provides one. Copy the fingers, not the volume. A recording that is loud does not mean you should blast.

When four notes are clean, play four slow B notes and four quicker ones. The note name stays B. Only the rhythm changes. Rest often so you do not become dizzy. Wipe the beak before you put the recorder down.

## Key words
• note B — the note played with the left thumb and the first finger only
• Baroque fingering — the standard fingering system used on many school descant recorders

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Which fingers cover holes for note B?

Working:
1. Thumb at the back.
2. Index finger on the first front hole.
3. No other fingers.

Answer: The left thumb and the left index finger.

## Worked examples

### Example 2
A player covers thumb, hole 1 and hole 2, and expects B. Which note are they fingering instead?

Working:
1. B is thumb and hole 1 only.
2. Adding hole 2 changes the note to A.

Answer: A

## Activity: Four clean B notes
You will need: Own descant recorder, Baroque fingering chart, A recording or teacher demonstration if available

1. Watch the demonstration of note B.

2. Finger B in silence and ask a partner to check thumb and index finger.

3. Play four slow tongued B notes.

4. Repair leaks or squeaks using the checklist.

5. Play four B notes again and put the recorder down to dry.

PAGE 14: Lesson 6: Playing the notes A and G — Note A

## Practice

1. How do you finger note B?

2. How many separate B notes are in a practice of four notes?

3. Give two reasons a B might squeak or fail.

## Answers to practice

1. Cover the left thumb hole and the first front hole only.

2. 4

3. Any two: leaking finger, thumb half covering, blowing too hard, hands swapped, head joint twisted.

## Summary
• B uses the left thumb and the index finger only.
• Tongue four steady notes with a gentle breath.
• Seal the holes and keep the window lined up.

LESSON 6: PLAYING THE NOTES A AND G
===================================

## What you will learn
• Finger A and G correctly.
• Move from B to A to G without twisting the recorder.
• Hear that G is the lowest of the three notes.

Curriculum outcomes: c) play notes B A and G on a descant recorder using appropriate playing techniques

## Introduction
Each new covered hole lowers the note. A adds one finger to B. G adds one more finger to A. The breath and the posture stay the same.

## Notes

Keep the left hand on top and the thumb sealed for all three notes.

### Note A
Cover the thumb hole, hole 1 and hole 2. Hole 2 is closed by the left middle finger. Hole 3 and the right-hand holes stay open. Play four tongued A notes. They should sound a step lower than B.

### Note G
Cover the thumb hole, hole 1, hole 2 and hole 3. Hole 3 is closed by the left ring finger. Play four tongued G notes. G is the lowest of these three notes. If G comes out higher than A, a hole is leaking or you have lifted a finger by mistake.

### Moving between them
The thumb and the index finger stay down for B, A and G. To go from B to A, add the middle finger. To go from A to G, add the ring finger. To climb back, lift one finger at a time. Do not take the whole hand off and replace it.

Practise this slow pattern: B A G, then G A B. Each note gets one gentle “doo”. Count four beats of rest before you repeat, so the class can hear the shape of the pattern.

PAGE 15: Lesson 6: Playing the notes A and G — Order of pitch

### Order of pitch
From highest to lowest the three notes are B, A, G. From lowest to highest they are G, A, B. Saying the letter as you play helps the ear check the finger. If the letter in your mouth and the sound in the air disagree, stop and look at the fingers.

Use a chart or a video only to check the fingers, then look up again. Staring at the holes while you play makes the recorder droop and the seal break.

## Key words
• note A — the note played with thumb and the first two fingers of the left hand
• note G — the note played with thumb and the first three fingers of the left hand

## Worked examples

### Example 1
How many front holes are covered for G?

Working:
1. G uses holes 1, 2 and 3.
2. That is three front holes, plus the thumb at the back.

Answer: Three front holes.

## Worked examples

### Example 2
Put B, A and G in order from lowest to highest.

Working:
1. Adding fingers lowers the note.
2. G has the most fingers covered, then A, then B.

Answer: G, A, B

## Activity: Step down and step up
You will need: Own descant recorder, Baroque fingering chart

1. Play four A notes, then four G notes, checking the chart if needed.

2. Play B A G slowly, one “doo” each.

3. Play G A B slowly.

4. A partner watches whether the thumb stays down.

5. Rest, dry the mouthpiece, and try the pattern once more.

PAGE 16: Lesson 7: Simple melodies on B, A and G

## Practice

1. Which fingers are down for note A?

2. Which note is lower, A or G?

3. Which finger do you add to change A into G?

## Answers to practice

1. Left thumb, index finger and middle finger.

2. G

3. The left ring finger.

## Summary
• A is thumb plus two fingers. G is thumb plus three fingers.
• The thumb stays down while you move between B, A and G.
• G is the lowest of the three notes and B is the highest.

LESSON 7: SIMPLE MELODIES ON B, A AND G
=======================================

## What you will learn
• Play a short melody using only B, A and G.
• Keep the rhythm steady.
• Breathe in places that do not break a short pattern.

Curriculum outcomes: d) play simple melodies based on notes B A and G on the descant recorder

## Introduction
Three notes are enough for a real tune. A melody is simply notes in an order, played in time. Hot Cross Buns is the tune many beginners use because it needs nothing lower than G.

PAGE 17: Lesson 7: Simple melodies on B, A and G — Accuracy

## Notes

A melody is a tune: notes one after another with a rhythm. You already have the only notes this melody needs.

### Hot Cross Buns
Sing or say the rhythm first, then play.

B A G
B A G
G G G G
A A A A
B A G

Each letter in a group of three is one steady beat. In the lines of four letters, each letter is also one beat, so those lines feel busier because the same kind of beat is filled with repeated notes. Do not rush the four Gs or the four As.

### How to practise
1. Say the letter names in rhythm while you clap.
2. Finger the notes in silence, still saying the letters.
3. Play only the first line: B A G.
4. Add the second line.
5. Add the repeated Gs and As.
6. Play the whole melody once. Stop. Breathe. Play it again.

Breathe before you start and, if you need air, after a line, not in the middle of “B A G”. A short melody should feel like one sentence.

### Accuracy
Pitch accuracy means G sounds lower than A, and A sounds lower than B. Rhythm accuracy means the beats stay even. If the class plays together, one person can count “1 2 3” for the three-note lines. Counting is part of keeping the rhythm, just as it is in gymnastics.

When the first melody is secure, try this four-beat pattern of your own using only these notes: G A B A. Repeat it four times. You have now played both a known tune and a small pattern you can control.

PAGE 18: Lesson 7: Simple melodies on B, A and G — Summary

## Key words
• melody — a tune made of notes in order
• beat — the steady pulse of the music

## Worked examples

### Example 1
The line “G G G G” has one note name on each beat. How many G notes is that?

Working:
1. Count the letters.
2. There are 4.

Answer: 4

## Worked examples

### Example 2
A player breathes between A and G in the first line, and the tune falls apart. Where is a better breath?

Working:
1. Do not break the three-note group.
2. Breathe before the line or after it.

Answer: Before the line or after the whole “B A G”.

## Activity: Play Hot Cross Buns
You will need: Own descant recorder, The letter pattern written on the board

1. Clap and say the letters in rhythm.

2. Finger the melody in silence.

3. Play one line at a time.

4. Play the whole melody slowly with a partner, starting together.

5. If the pitch slips, stop and play B, A and G alone before you try the tune again.

## Practice

1. Which three notes does Hot Cross Buns use in this lesson?

2. Write the first two lines of the melody as note letters.

3. What does rhythm accuracy mean here?

## Answers to practice

1. B, A and G.

2. B A G / B A G

3. The beats stay even and the notes stay in time.

## Summary
• Say and clap the rhythm before you play.
• Hot Cross Buns uses B, A and G only.
• Breathe between lines, and keep the beats even.

PAGE 19: Lesson 8: Playing together and giving feedback — What to watch and hear

LESSON 8: PLAYING TOGETHER AND GIVING FEEDBACK
==============================================

## What you will learn
• Play a melody with a partner or a small group.
• Comment on tone, fingering and rhythm kindly.
• Show that you enjoy playing and that you care for the recorder afterwards.

Curriculum outcomes: d) play simple melodies based on notes B A and G on the descant recorder; e) enjoy playing melodies using the descant recorder

## Introduction
A tune played alone is practice. A tune played with others, and then talked about fairly, is a performance. You can enjoy the sound and still help someone improve.

## Notes

Sit in a small group. Choose a leader to count “1, 2, ready, play”. Everyone starts on the same beat and plays Hot Cross Buns, or the pattern G A B A repeated. Listening is as important as blowing. If you cannot hear the group, you are too loud.

### What to watch and hear
- **Tone:** gentle and clear, or squeaky and forced?
- **Fingering:** did B, A and G sound in the right order, high to low?
- **Rhythm:** did the four repeated notes stay even?
- **Posture:** tall body, left hand on top, recorder slanting, no biting?
- **Care:** own instrument only, dry at the end?

PAGE 20: Lesson 8: Playing together and giving feedback — Enjoyment

### Feedback
Use two sentences.

- “I heard a clear tone on the Gs.”
- “Next time, keep the beats of the four As more even.”

Do not grab another person’s recorder to show them. Mime the fingers on your own. Accept feedback without arguing. Then play the melody once more, trying only the one change that was asked for.

### Enjoyment
The recorder is enjoyable when the tone is pleasant and the group starts together. That pleasure grows with short, regular practice, not with one long noisy session. When you finish, wipe the beak, shake out moisture, take the joints apart gently if that is your class routine, and store the recorder in its case. Thank the group. Playing well and looking after the instrument belong in the same lesson.

## Key words
• ensemble — a group playing together
• feedback — comments that say what worked and what to improve

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A group of 5 players each plays the melody twice. How many play-throughs does the group make in total?

Working:
1. 5 players × 2 = 10

Answer: 10

## Worked examples

### Example 2
Someone says, “That was awful.” Rewrite it as useful feedback.

Working:
1. Name one good point.
2. Give one next step.

Answer: Example: “I heard the B A G in the right order. Next time, soften the breath so the tone does not squeak.”

## Activity: Play, listen, improve
You will need: Own descant recorders, Space to sit in groups of four

1. The leader counts the group in and you play the melody together.

2. Listeners use the two-sentence feedback.

3. Play once more, changing only the point that was mentioned.

4. Swap so another learner leads.

5. Dry and store the recorders. Say one thing you enjoyed.

## Practice

1. What should a leader do before the group plays?

2. Name two things you can comment on.

3. What do you do with the recorder at the end?

## Answers to practice

1. Count everyone in so they start together.

2. Any two: tone, fingering, rhythm, posture, care of the instrument.

3. Wipe it, let the moisture out, and store it in its case.

## Summary
• Start together and listen to the group.
• Give one strength and one next step.
• Enjoy the tune, then clean and store the recorder.

PAGE 21: Revision quiz

REVISION QUIZ
=============

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. Which joint has the beak and the window?
   A. Foot joint
   B. Middle joint
   C. Head joint
   D. The strap

2. Which hand goes nearer the beak?
   A. Right hand
   B. Left hand
   C. Either hand
   D. Neither; the recorder is held in one fist

3. Why must you not share a recorder mouthpiece?

4. A plastic recorder should be washed in…
   A. boiling water
   B. lukewarm soapy water, then rinsed and dried
   C. a puddle
   D. oil

5. A good tone is produced by…
   A. blowing as hard as possible
   B. a gentle steady breath, tonguing, and sealed holes
   C. biting the beak
   D. covering the window with a finger

6. Note B is fingered with…
   A. thumb and index finger
   B. all fingers of both hands
   C. no fingers at all
   D. only the right hand

7. Which note is the lowest: B, A or G?
   A. B
   B. A
   C. G
   D. They are the same

8. Which pattern is the first line of Hot Cross Buns in this lesson?
   A. G B A
   B. B A G
   C. A A A A
   D. C D E

9. Where should you breathe in a short “B A G” line?

10. Which of these is useful feedback after a recorder performance?
   A. “That was awful.”
   B. “I heard a clear G. Next time, keep the four As more even.”
   C. “Give me your recorder.”
   D. “Stop playing forever.”

PAGE 22: Quiz answers

ANSWERS
=======

1. C. Head joint
   The head joint is the top piece with the mouthpiece and the window.

2. B. Left hand
   The left hand plays the upper holes for B, A and G.

3. Germs can pass from one person to another and spread communicable diseases.
   Hygiene protects the class.

4. B. lukewarm soapy water, then rinsed and dried
   Lukewarm water cleans it without warping it. It must be dried afterwards.

5. B. a gentle steady breath, tonguing, and sealed holes
   Gentle air, a clean tongue start and no leaks make a clear tone.

6. A. thumb and index finger
   B uses the left thumb and the first front hole.

7. C. G
   G uses the most fingers of the three and sounds the lowest.

8. B. B A G
   The melody begins B A G, then repeats that pattern.

9. Before the line or after it, not between the notes of the group.
   A breath in the middle breaks the melody.

10. B. “I heard a clear G. Next time, keep the four As more even.”
   Feedback names a strength and one improvement.

studyPages.title: Overview
studyPages.body:
OVERVIEW
========

The descant recorder is a small wind instrument played with the mouth and the fingers. In this sub-strand you will name its parts, learn how to keep it clean and store it safely, and play the notes B, A and G with a good posture and a gentle breath. You will then play simple tunes on those three notes and listen to one another.

## Strand 2.0: Performing and Displaying
Sub-strand 2.5: Descant Recorder
Suggested lessons: 15

## What this sub-strand covers
• Parts: head joint, middle joint, foot joint, finger holes
• Care: hygiene measures, handling and storage
• Techniques: posture, fingering and blowing

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 Creative Arts Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Strand 2.0 Performing and Displaying, Sub-strand 2.5 Descant Recorder

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) identify the parts of a descant recorder for familiarisation
b) care for a descant recorder for longevity
c) play notes B A and G on a descant recorder using appropriate playing techniques
d) play simple melodies based on notes B A and G on the descant recorder
e) enjoy playing melodies using the descant recorder

## Key inquiry questions
1. How can a good tone be produced on the descant recorder?

studyPages.title: How we will learn
studyPages.body:
## Learning experiences
• familiarise with the descant recorder to identify its parts
• brainstorm on ways of caring for a descant recorder and its importance
• practise the techniques of playing a descant recorder
• use digital devices responsibly to search and watch recordings/ watch live demonstrations on how to play notes B A and G on the descant recorder
• play simple melodies based on B A and G on the descant recorder with accuracy in pitch and rhythm applying the playing techniques
• watch peers play melodies on the descant recorder, critique and give feedback to peers for improvement

## Core competencies
• Digital literacy: The learner uses digital devices to search and watch how to play notes on the descant recorder
• Learning to learn: The learner searches for and acquires skills of how to play new notes on the descant recorder

## Values
• Respect: The learner listens to and accommodates peers’ views during discussions
• Responsibility: The learner takes care of the descant recorder during and after use

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Communicable diseases: The learner prevents the spread of communicable diseases by observing hygiene measures in the use of the descant recorder
• Social cohesion: The learner plays the descant recorder with peers in a group

## Links to other learning areas
• Agriculture: The learner applies the concepts and knowledge learnt on prevention of communicable diseases in the use of the descant recorder

studyPages.title: Lesson 1: Parts of the descant recorder — The three joints
studyPages.body:
LESSON 1: PARTS OF THE DESCANT RECORDER
=======================================

## What you will learn
• Name the head joint, middle joint, foot joint and finger holes.
• Assemble the recorder so the holes line up.
• Hold it the right way up before any playing.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify the parts of a descant recorder for familiarisation

## Introduction
A descant recorder looks like one tube, but it comes apart into pieces. If you do not know which piece is which, you cannot put it together or find the notes.

## Notes

The descant recorder is the small recorder most schools use. It is sometimes called a soprano recorder. Sound is made by blowing gently into the mouthpiece while fingers cover and uncover holes. Covering more holes makes a lower note.

### The three joints
- The **head joint** is the top piece. It has the **beak** (the mouthpiece you rest on your lips) and the **window**, a rectangular opening underneath where the air splits and the sound begins.
- The **middle joint** is the long middle piece. Most of the finger holes are on it.
- The **foot joint** is the small bottom piece. It has the last hole, often a double hole.

### Finger holes
The holes on the front are covered by the fingers. The hole at the back of the head joint, or at the top of the middle joint depending on the model, is covered by the left thumb. You do not need every hole yet. Notes B, A and G use only the left thumb and the first fingers of the left hand. The other holes still have to be there, and you must not block them by mistake.

studyPages.title: Lesson 1: Parts of the descant recorder — Example 2
studyPages.body:
### Putting it together
Fit the foot joint onto the middle joint, then fit the head joint. Use a gentle twist. Do not force the pieces or bang them on a desk. The window of the head joint should line up with the finger holes. If the head joint faces sideways, your fingers will not sit on the holes.

Left hand goes at the top, nearer the beak. Right hand goes at the bottom. If you swap hands, the notes B, A and G will not work. Look at a chart or a real recorder and touch each part as you name it. Familiarity means you can name the parts without looking at a label.

## Key words
• descant recorder — a small recorder played by blowing and covering finger holes
• head joint — the top piece with the beak and the window
• middle joint — the long piece with most of the finger holes
• foot joint — the small bottom piece
• finger hole — an opening covered by a finger to change the note

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Which joint has the beak and the window?

Working:
1. The mouthpiece is at the top.
2. The top piece is the head joint.

Answer: The head joint.

## Worked examples

### Example 2
A learner puts the right hand at the top. What will go wrong?

Working:
1. The left hand must be nearer the beak.
2. Notes B, A and G use the left-hand fingers.

Answer: The fingers will be on the wrong holes, so B, A and G will not sound correctly.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Caring for the recorder — Hygiene
studyPages.body:
## Activity: Name and assemble
You will need: A descant recorder for each player or for each pair, A diagram or Baroque fingering chart

1. Take the recorder apart carefully.

2. Point to the head joint, middle joint, foot joint, beak, window and finger holes.

3. Assemble it with a gentle twist so the window lines up with the holes.

4. Place the left hand at the top and the right hand below, without playing yet.

5. Your partner checks the lineup and the hands.

## Practice

1. Name the three joints of a descant recorder from top to bottom.

2. What is the window?

3. Which hand goes nearer the beak?

## Answers to practice

1. Head joint, middle joint, foot joint.

2. The rectangular opening where the air splits and the sound begins.

3. The left hand.

## Summary
• The recorder has a head joint, a middle joint and a foot joint.
• Finger holes change the notes.
• Assemble it gently, with the left hand at the top.

LESSON 2: CARING FOR THE RECORDER
=================================

## What you will learn
• Clean and store a descant recorder correctly.
• Explain how hygiene stops germs spreading.
• Give two reasons why care makes the instrument last.

Curriculum outcomes: b) care for a descant recorder for longevity

## Introduction
A recorder goes in the mouth, so it is not like a drum that the whole class can hit in turn. How you clean it, hold it and put it away decides both its life and the health of the class.

## Notes

Care has two aims. Hygiene keeps germs from spreading. Gentle handling and storage make the recorder last. Lasting a long time is what longevity means.

### Hygiene
- Play only your own recorder. Do not lend the beak to a friend “just to try”.
- Wash your hands before you play.
- Do not play if you have a mouth infection, and do not share mouthpieces when someone has a cold or a cough. This helps prevent communicable diseases, the illnesses that pass from person to person.
- After playing, shake moisture out of the head joint. Wipe the beak.
- A plastic school recorder may be washed in lukewarm soapy water, rinsed and dried. Do not use boiling water. Do not leave it to soak all day.
- If your recorder is wooden, do not soak it. Wipe it and let it dry. Ask the teacher before washing any recorder that is not plastic.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Caring for the recorder — Example 1
studyPages.body:
### Handling
- Do not bite the beak.
- Do not bang the joints together or use the recorder as a pointer.
- Twist gently when you take it apart. Forcing a stuck joint can crack it.
- Carry it in your hand or case, not in a pocket full of pens.

### Storage
- Dry it before you put it away.
- Keep it in a case or a clean bag.
- Do not leave it in hot sun or on a window sill. Heat can warp plastic and crack wood.
- Store it where it will not be sat on.

A dirty, shared, sun-baked recorder becomes unpleasant to play and may not sound. A clean, personal, cool, dry recorder is ready for the next lesson.

## Key words
• hygiene — clean habits that stop germs spreading
• longevity — a long life; here, the recorder lasting a long time
• communicable disease — an illness that can pass from one person to another

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Two learners have a cold and want to try each other’s recorders. Why is that a poor idea?

Working:
1. Colds spread through shared mouthpieces.
2. Each player should use only their own recorder.

Answer: They could pass germs to each other. Each person should play only their own recorder.

## Worked examples

### Example 2
A plastic recorder was left on a hot window sill. What risk is that?

Working:
1. Heat can bend plastic.

Answer: The recorder may warp, so the joints and holes no longer fit well.

## Activity: Clean, dry and store
You will need: Own descant recorder, Lukewarm soapy water if the teacher says the recorder is plastic, Clean cloth, Case or clean bag

1. In a group, list ways of caring for the recorder and why each one matters.

2. Wash hands. If the recorder is plastic and the teacher agrees, wash it in lukewarm soapy water and rinse it.

3. Dry the joints and the beak.

4. Assemble it gently, then take it apart again and put it in the case.

5. Agree one class rule: nobody shares a mouthpiece.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Posture and how to hold the recorder — Body
studyPages.body:
## Practice

1. Why should learners not share recorder mouthpieces?

2. What water is safe for a plastic recorder?

3. Give two storage rules.

## Answers to practice

1. Germs that cause communicable diseases can spread from mouth to mouth.

2. Lukewarm soapy water, followed by a rinse and drying. Not boiling water.

3. Any two: dry it first, use a case or clean bag, keep it out of hot sun, do not leave it where it can be sat on.

## Summary
• Play only your own recorder and wash your hands.
• Wash a plastic recorder in lukewarm water, then dry it.
• Store it cool, dry and protected so it lasts.

LESSON 3: POSTURE AND HOW TO HOLD THE RECORDER
==============================================

## What you will learn
• Sit or stand with a playing posture.
• Place the left hand on top and seal the holes with the pads of the fingers.
• Support the recorder with the right hand without covering holes you do not need.

Curriculum outcomes: c) play notes B A and G on a descant recorder using appropriate playing techniques

## Introduction
A hunched back and flat fingers make the recorder squeak before the tune has started. Posture is the first playing technique.

## Notes

Posture means the way you sit or stand and the way you hold the instrument. A good posture lets the breath move and lets the fingers seal the holes.

### Body
- Sit toward the front of the chair, or stand with both feet on the ground.
- Keep the back tall, not stiff. The shoulders stay down.
- The head is level. Do not tuck the chin hard into the chest.
- Hold the recorder at a slant, pointing down and slightly forward, about halfway between straight up and straight out. It should not point at the floor between your feet, and it should not stick straight out like a stick.

### Hands
- Left hand on top. The left thumb covers the thumb hole at the back.
- The pads of the fingers, not the very tips and not the flat middle of the finger, cover the holes.
- Fingers are curved, as if each hand is holding a small ball.
- Right hand supports the lower joint. For notes B, A and G the right-hand fingers stay just above their holes, ready, but they do not cover them.
- Elbows hang relaxed. Do not glue them to your ribs and do not flap them out.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Posture and how to hold the recorder — Silent holding practice
studyPages.body:
### A seal test
Cover one hole and ask a partner to look around the finger. If they can see the hole, air will leak and the note will be wrong or noisy. Leaks are the main reason beginners think the recorder is broken.

Practise the holding shape in silence. Lifting and replacing one finger without looking at the hole is the skill you will need when the notes arrive. Keep the recorder out of your mouth until the next lesson, so that posture is learnt before blowing.

## Key words
• posture — the way you sit or stand and hold the instrument
• pad of the finger — the soft front of the fingertip that seals a hole
• seal — to cover a hole completely so air cannot leak

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner’s note will not sound and a partner can see half of hole 1. What is the cause?

Working:
1. A visible hole means air is leaking.
2. The pad of the finger must seal it.

Answer: The finger is not sealing the hole.

## Worked examples

### Example 2
Which hand is on top when playing B, A and G?

Working:
1. Those notes use the upper holes.
2. The left hand plays the upper holes.

Answer: The left hand.

## Activity: Silent holding practice
You will need: Descant recorder, Chair or standing space, A partner

1. Sit or stand tall and hold the recorder at a comfortable downward slant.

2. Place the left thumb and fingers in a curved shape. The right hand supports the bottom.

3. Your partner checks that the left hand is on top and that covered holes are fully sealed.

4. Lift one finger and replace it five times without twisting the recorder.

5. Rest the recorder in your lap or case. Nobody blows yet.

studyPages.title: Lesson 4: Blowing and a good tone
studyPages.body:
## Practice

1. Where should the left hand be?

2. Which part of the finger seals a hole?

3. What does the right hand do while you play B, A and G?

## Answers to practice

1. At the top, nearer the beak.

2. The pad of the finger.

3. It supports the lower part of the recorder and stays ready, without covering holes.

## Summary
• Sit or stand tall, with the recorder slanting gently downward.
• Left hand on top, fingers curved, holes sealed.
• The right hand supports the instrument for these three notes.

LESSON 4: BLOWING AND A GOOD TONE
=================================

## What you will learn
• Start a sound with the tongue.
• Use a gentle, steady breath.
• Explain what causes a squeak.

Curriculum outcomes: c) play notes B A and G on a descant recorder using appropriate playing techniques

## Introduction
The recorder does not need the huge breath you use to blow up a ball. It needs a small, steady stream of air, started neatly with the tongue.

## Notes

Tone is the quality of the sound: clear, gentle and steady, or squeaky, breathy and harsh. The question for this instrument is how a good tone is produced.

### The mouth
Rest the beak on the lower lip and close the lips gently around it. Do not bite. Only a small part of the beak goes into the mouth. The teeth do not clamp down. The cheeks stay flat, not puffed out.

studyPages.title: Lesson 4: Blowing and a good tone — A first sound
studyPages.body:
### The tongue
Start each note by saying “doo” or “too” inside the mouth. The tongue touches the back of the upper teeth and comes away as the air begins. This is called tonguing. It makes a clean start. Blowing without the tongue makes a fuzzy “whoosh”.

### The breath
Blow warm, slow air, as if you were steaming a mirror. If you blow hard, the recorder jumps to a high squeak. If you blow too little, you get a whisper and no note. Steady air in the middle is the tone you want.

### A first sound
Cover no front holes. Cover the thumb hole only if your teacher’s chart asks for that first open note. Many classes first practise a gentle tongued sound so the ears learn a clear tone before the fingers complicate it. If the sound squeaks:

- blow more gently
- check that you are not biting
- check for leaking fingers if any holes are covered
- check that the head joint window is lined up and not blocked by dirt

Stop every few minutes and let moisture out of the head joint. A blocked window gurgles. Good tone is gentle air, a tongued start, a sealed hole and a clear window.

studyPages.title: Lesson 4: Blowing and a good tone — Answers to practice
studyPages.body:
## Key words
• tone — the quality of the sound
• tonguing — starting a note with the tongue, as in “doo” or “too”
• squeak — a high unwanted sound caused by blowing too hard or by a leak

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Every note jumps to a high squeak. What should the player change first?

Working:
1. Hard blowing makes the recorder overblow.
2. The breath should be gentle and steady.

Answer: Blow more gently, with warm steady air.

## Worked examples

### Example 2
The sound starts with a fuzzy whoosh. Which technique is missing?

Working:
1. A clean start uses the tongue.
2. Saying “doo” or “too” is tonguing.

Answer: Tonguing.

## Activity: Gentle “doo” sounds
You will need: Own descant recorder

1. Check posture and a clean beak.

2. Practise saying “doo doo doo doo” on a gentle breath, four sounds, then rest.

3. If the sound squeaks, soften the breath and try again.

4. A partner says whether the tone was clear or forced.

5. Shake moisture out and rest the recorder.

## Practice

1. How can a good tone be produced on the descant recorder?

2. What happens if you blow too hard?

3. Should you bite the beak?

## Answers to practice

1. Use a gentle steady breath, start the note with the tongue, seal the holes, and keep the window clear.

2. The note squeaks or jumps too high.

3. No. The lips rest gently around it.

## Summary
• Lips rest gently on the beak. Do not bite or puff the cheeks.
• Start notes with “doo” or “too”.
• A gentle steady breath makes a clear tone.

studyPages.title: Lesson 5: Playing the note B — Steps
studyPages.body:
LESSON 5: PLAYING THE NOTE B
============================

## What you will learn
• Finger note B on a Baroque descant recorder.
• Play four steady B notes with a clear tone.
• Fix a leak or a squeak on B.

Curriculum outcomes: c) play notes B A and G on a descant recorder using appropriate playing techniques

## Introduction
B is the first of the three notes in this sub-strand. It uses the fewest fingers, so it is the best place to join posture, breath and a sealed hole.

## Notes

Use a Baroque fingering chart, the chart used with school descant recorders in this design. For note B, only two holes are covered:

- the left thumb covers the thumb hole at the back
- the left index finger covers hole 1, the first hole on the front

All the other holes stay open. The right hand still supports the recorder.

### Steps
1. Sit or stand tall. Left hand on top.
2. Seal the thumb hole and hole 1. Look once to check, then look forward.
3. Start with “doo” and a gentle breath.
4. Hold the note while you count “one”, then stop the air with the tongue.
5. Play four separate B notes: doo, doo, doo, doo. Keep them the same length.

studyPages.title: Lesson 5: Playing the note B — Four clean B notes
studyPages.body:
### If B will not sound
- The index finger is leaking. Seal with the pad.
- The thumb is only half on the hole.
- You are blowing too hard.
- You swapped hands.
- The head joint has twisted so the window is no longer in line.

Watch a live demonstration or a recording if the teacher provides one. Copy the fingers, not the volume. A recording that is loud does not mean you should blast.

When four notes are clean, play four slow B notes and four quicker ones. The note name stays B. Only the rhythm changes. Rest often so you do not become dizzy. Wipe the beak before you put the recorder down.

## Key words
• note B — the note played with the left thumb and the first finger only
• Baroque fingering — the standard fingering system used on many school descant recorders

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Which fingers cover holes for note B?

Working:
1. Thumb at the back.
2. Index finger on the first front hole.
3. No other fingers.

Answer: The left thumb and the left index finger.

## Worked examples

### Example 2
A player covers thumb, hole 1 and hole 2, and expects B. Which note are they fingering instead?

Working:
1. B is thumb and hole 1 only.
2. Adding hole 2 changes the note to A.

Answer: A

## Activity: Four clean B notes
You will need: Own descant recorder, Baroque fingering chart, A recording or teacher demonstration if available

1. Watch the demonstration of note B.

2. Finger B in silence and ask a partner to check thumb and index finger.

3. Play four slow tongued B notes.

4. Repair leaks or squeaks using the checklist.

5. Play four B notes again and put the recorder down to dry.

studyPages.title: Lesson 6: Playing the notes A and G — Note A
studyPages.body:
## Practice

1. How do you finger note B?

2. How many separate B notes are in a practice of four notes?

3. Give two reasons a B might squeak or fail.

## Answers to practice

1. Cover the left thumb hole and the first front hole only.

2. 4

3. Any two: leaking finger, thumb half covering, blowing too hard, hands swapped, head joint twisted.

## Summary
• B uses the left thumb and the index finger only.
• Tongue four steady notes with a gentle breath.
• Seal the holes and keep the window lined up.

LESSON 6: PLAYING THE NOTES A AND G
===================================

## What you will learn
• Finger A and G correctly.
• Move from B to A to G without twisting the recorder.
• Hear that G is the lowest of the three notes.

Curriculum outcomes: c) play notes B A and G on a descant recorder using appropriate playing techniques

## Introduction
Each new covered hole lowers the note. A adds one finger to B. G adds one more finger to A. The breath and the posture stay the same.

## Notes

Keep the left hand on top and the thumb sealed for all three notes.

### Note A
Cover the thumb hole, hole 1 and hole 2. Hole 2 is closed by the left middle finger. Hole 3 and the right-hand holes stay open. Play four tongued A notes. They should sound a step lower than B.

### Note G
Cover the thumb hole, hole 1, hole 2 and hole 3. Hole 3 is closed by the left ring finger. Play four tongued G notes. G is the lowest of these three notes. If G comes out higher than A, a hole is leaking or you have lifted a finger by mistake.

### Moving between them
The thumb and the index finger stay down for B, A and G. To go from B to A, add the middle finger. To go from A to G, add the ring finger. To climb back, lift one finger at a time. Do not take the whole hand off and replace it.

Practise this slow pattern: B A G, then G A B. Each note gets one gentle “doo”. Count four beats of rest before you repeat, so the class can hear the shape of the pattern.

studyPages.title: Lesson 6: Playing the notes A and G — Order of pitch
studyPages.body:
### Order of pitch
From highest to lowest the three notes are B, A, G. From lowest to highest they are G, A, B. Saying the letter as you play helps the ear check the finger. If the letter in your mouth and the sound in the air disagree, stop and look at the fingers.

Use a chart or a video only to check the fingers, then look up again. Staring at the holes while you play makes the recorder droop and the seal break.

## Key words
• note A — the note played with thumb and the first two fingers of the left hand
• note G — the note played with thumb and the first three fingers of the left hand

## Worked examples

### Example 1
How many front holes are covered for G?

Working:
1. G uses holes 1, 2 and 3.
2. That is three front holes, plus the thumb at the back.

Answer: Three front holes.

## Worked examples

### Example 2
Put B, A and G in order from lowest to highest.

Working:
1. Adding fingers lowers the note.
2. G has the most fingers covered, then A, then B.

Answer: G, A, B

## Activity: Step down and step up
You will need: Own descant recorder, Baroque fingering chart

1. Play four A notes, then four G notes, checking the chart if needed.

2. Play B A G slowly, one “doo” each.

3. Play G A B slowly.

4. A partner watches whether the thumb stays down.

5. Rest, dry the mouthpiece, and try the pattern once more.

studyPages.title: Lesson 7: Simple melodies on B, A and G
studyPages.body:
## Practice

1. Which fingers are down for note A?

2. Which note is lower, A or G?

3. Which finger do you add to change A into G?

## Answers to practice

1. Left thumb, index finger and middle finger.

2. G

3. The left ring finger.

## Summary
• A is thumb plus two fingers. G is thumb plus three fingers.
• The thumb stays down while you move between B, A and G.
• G is the lowest of the three notes and B is the highest.

LESSON 7: SIMPLE MELODIES ON B, A AND G
=======================================

## What you will learn
• Play a short melody using only B, A and G.
• Keep the rhythm steady.
• Breathe in places that do not break a short pattern.

Curriculum outcomes: d) play simple melodies based on notes B A and G on the descant recorder

## Introduction
Three notes are enough for a real tune. A melody is simply notes in an order, played in time. Hot Cross Buns is the tune many beginners use because it needs nothing lower than G.

studyPages.title: Lesson 7: Simple melodies on B, A and G — Accuracy
studyPages.body:
## Notes

A melody is a tune: notes one after another with a rhythm. You already have the only notes this melody needs.

### Hot Cross Buns
Sing or say the rhythm first, then play.

B A G
B A G
G G G G
A A A A
B A G

Each letter in a group of three is one steady beat. In the lines of four letters, each letter is also one beat, so those lines feel busier because the same kind of beat is filled with repeated notes. Do not rush the four Gs or the four As.

### How to practise
1. Say the letter names in rhythm while you clap.
2. Finger the notes in silence, still saying the letters.
3. Play only the first line: B A G.
4. Add the second line.
5. Add the repeated Gs and As.
6. Play the whole melody once. Stop. Breathe. Play it again.

Breathe before you start and, if you need air, after a line, not in the middle of “B A G”. A short melody should feel like one sentence.

### Accuracy
Pitch accuracy means G sounds lower than A, and A sounds lower than B. Rhythm accuracy means the beats stay even. If the class plays together, one person can count “1 2 3” for the three-note lines. Counting is part of keeping the rhythm, just as it is in gymnastics.

When the first melody is secure, try this four-beat pattern of your own using only these notes: G A B A. Repeat it four times. You have now played both a known tune and a small pattern you can control.

studyPages.title: Lesson 7: Simple melodies on B, A and G — Summary
studyPages.body:
## Key words
• melody — a tune made of notes in order
• beat — the steady pulse of the music

## Worked examples

### Example 1
The line “G G G G” has one note name on each beat. How many G notes is that?

Working:
1. Count the letters.
2. There are 4.

Answer: 4

## Worked examples

### Example 2
A player breathes between A and G in the first line, and the tune falls apart. Where is a better breath?

Working:
1. Do not break the three-note group.
2. Breathe before the line or after it.

Answer: Before the line or after the whole “B A G”.

## Activity: Play Hot Cross Buns
You will need: Own descant recorder, The letter pattern written on the board

1. Clap and say the letters in rhythm.

2. Finger the melody in silence.

3. Play one line at a time.

4. Play the whole melody slowly with a partner, starting together.

5. If the pitch slips, stop and play B, A and G alone before you try the tune again.

## Practice

1. Which three notes does Hot Cross Buns use in this lesson?

2. Write the first two lines of the melody as note letters.

3. What does rhythm accuracy mean here?

## Answers to practice

1. B, A and G.

2. B A G / B A G

3. The beats stay even and the notes stay in time.

## Summary
• Say and clap the rhythm before you play.
• Hot Cross Buns uses B, A and G only.
• Breathe between lines, and keep the beats even.

studyPages.title: Lesson 8: Playing together and giving feedback — What to watch and hear
studyPages.body:
LESSON 8: PLAYING TOGETHER AND GIVING FEEDBACK
==============================================

## What you will learn
• Play a melody with a partner or a small group.
• Comment on tone, fingering and rhythm kindly.
• Show that you enjoy playing and that you care for the recorder afterwards.

Curriculum outcomes: d) play simple melodies based on notes B A and G on the descant recorder; e) enjoy playing melodies using the descant recorder

## Introduction
A tune played alone is practice. A tune played with others, and then talked about fairly, is a performance. You can enjoy the sound and still help someone improve.

## Notes

Sit in a small group. Choose a leader to count “1, 2, ready, play”. Everyone starts on the same beat and plays Hot Cross Buns, or the pattern G A B A repeated. Listening is as important as blowing. If you cannot hear the group, you are too loud.

### What to watch and hear
- **Tone:** gentle and clear, or squeaky and forced?
- **Fingering:** did B, A and G sound in the right order, high to low?
- **Rhythm:** did the four repeated notes stay even?
- **Posture:** tall body, left hand on top, recorder slanting, no biting?
- **Care:** own instrument only, dry at the end?

studyPages.title: Lesson 8: Playing together and giving feedback — Enjoyment
studyPages.body:
### Feedback
Use two sentences.

- “I heard a clear tone on the Gs.”
- “Next time, keep the beats of the four As more even.”

Do not grab another person’s recorder to show them. Mime the fingers on your own. Accept feedback without arguing. Then play the melody once more, trying only the one change that was asked for.

### Enjoyment
The recorder is enjoyable when the tone is pleasant and the group starts together. That pleasure grows with short, regular practice, not with one long noisy session. When you finish, wipe the beak, shake out moisture, take the joints apart gently if that is your class routine, and store the recorder in its case. Thank the group. Playing well and looking after the instrument belong in the same lesson.

## Key words
• ensemble — a group playing together
• feedback — comments that say what worked and what to improve

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A group of 5 players each plays the melody twice. How many play-throughs does the group make in total?

Working:
1. 5 players × 2 = 10

Answer: 10

## Worked examples

### Example 2
Someone says, “That was awful.” Rewrite it as useful feedback.

Working:
1. Name one good point.
2. Give one next step.

Answer: Example: “I heard the B A G in the right order. Next time, soften the breath so the tone does not squeak.”

## Activity: Play, listen, improve
You will need: Own descant recorders, Space to sit in groups of four

1. The leader counts the group in and you play the melody together.

2. Listeners use the two-sentence feedback.

3. Play once more, changing only the point that was mentioned.

4. Swap so another learner leads.

5. Dry and store the recorders. Say one thing you enjoyed.

## Practice

1. What should a leader do before the group plays?

2. Name two things you can comment on.

3. What do you do with the recorder at the end?

## Answers to practice

1. Count everyone in so they start together.

2. Any two: tone, fingering, rhythm, posture, care of the instrument.

3. Wipe it, let the moisture out, and store it in its case.

## Summary
• Start together and listen to the group.
• Give one strength and one next step.
• Enjoy the tune, then clean and store the recorder.

studyPages.title: Revision quiz
studyPages.body:
REVISION QUIZ
=============

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. Which joint has the beak and the window?
   A. Foot joint
   B. Middle joint
   C. Head joint
   D. The strap

2. Which hand goes nearer the beak?
   A. Right hand
   B. Left hand
   C. Either hand
   D. Neither; the recorder is held in one fist

3. Why must you not share a recorder mouthpiece?

4. A plastic recorder should be washed in…
   A. boiling water
   B. lukewarm soapy water, then rinsed and dried
   C. a puddle
   D. oil

5. A good tone is produced by…
   A. blowing as hard as possible
   B. a gentle steady breath, tonguing, and sealed holes
   C. biting the beak
   D. covering the window with a finger

6. Note B is fingered with…
   A. thumb and index finger
   B. all fingers of both hands
   C. no fingers at all
   D. only the right hand

7. Which note is the lowest: B, A or G?
   A. B
   B. A
   C. G
   D. They are the same

8. Which pattern is the first line of Hot Cross Buns in this lesson?
   A. G B A
   B. B A G
   C. A A A A
   D. C D E

9. Where should you breathe in a short “B A G” line?

10. Which of these is useful feedback after a recorder performance?
   A. “That was awful.”
   B. “I heard a clear G. Next time, keep the four As more even.”
   C. “Give me your recorder.”
   D. “Stop playing forever.”

studyPages.title: Quiz answers
studyPages.body:
ANSWERS
=======

1. C. Head joint
   The head joint is the top piece with the mouthpiece and the window.

2. B. Left hand
   The left hand plays the upper holes for B, A and G.

3. Germs can pass from one person to another and spread communicable diseases.
   Hygiene protects the class.

4. B. lukewarm soapy water, then rinsed and dried
   Lukewarm water cleans it without warping it. It must be dried afterwards.

5. B. a gentle steady breath, tonguing, and sealed holes
   Gentle air, a clean tongue start and no leaks make a clear tone.

6. A. thumb and index finger
   B uses the left thumb and the first front hole.

7. C. G
   G uses the most fingers of the three and sounds the lowest.

8. B. B A G
   The melody begins B A G, then repeats that pattern.

9. Before the line or after it, not between the notes of the group.
   A breath in the middle breaks the melody.

10. B. “I heard a clear G. Next time, keep the four As more even.”
   Feedback names a strength and one improvement.
